title: AP Calculus BC
description: Free AP Calculus BC study guide: limits, differentiation, integration and differential equations, applications of integration, parametric, polar and vector functions, and infinite series through Taylor polynomials and error bounds. 132 practice questions with explanations, 66 flashcards and a practice exam.

units.name: Limits & Continuity

concepts.intro: A limit describes the value f(x) approaches as x gets close to a number, not necessarily the value at that number.
b: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a (x ≠ a)
The limit exists only if the left-hand and right-hand limits both exist and are equal
A limit can exist even when f(a) is undefined, e.g. a hole in the graph
Infinite limits (vertical asymptotes) and limits at infinity (horizontal asymptotes) describe unbounded or end behavior
Estimate limits from graphs and tables, then confirm algebraically

concepts.intro: Most limits come from direct substitution or a little algebra to remove a 0/0 form.
b: If f is continuous at a, lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a): just substitute
0/0 is indeterminate: factor and cancel, rationalize, or combine fractions, then substitute
Special limits: lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1 and lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x = 0
Limits at infinity of rational functions: compare the degrees of numerator and denominator
The Squeeze Theorem: if g ≤ f ≤ h and g and h share a limit L, then f → L too

concepts.intro: A function is continuous at a point when there is no break, jump or hole there.
b: f is continuous at a if f(a) is defined, lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and the two are equal
Discontinuities: removable (hole), jump (one-sided limits differ), infinite (vertical asymptote)
Polynomials, rational functions (on their domains), exponentials, logs and trig functions are continuous where defined
Intermediate Value Theorem: if f is continuous on [a, b], it takes every value between f(a) and f(b)
The IVT guarantees a root exists when a continuous function changes sign on an interval

keyFacts: A limit exists only when the left- and right-hand limits agree.
Continuity at a: f(a) defined, the limit exists, and they're equal.
IVT needs continuity on a closed interval.
traps: 0/0 doesn't mean the limit is 0 or undefined. It means you need more algebra.
f(a) and lim_{x→a} f(x) can differ; the limit ignores the value at a.
The IVT says a value exists, not where it is or how many times it's hit.

units.name: Differentiation & Applications

concepts.intro: The derivative measures instantaneous rate of change: the slope of the tangent line.
b: f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h
Average rate of change on [a, b] is [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a), the slope of a secant line
The derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent line there
Differentiable implies continuous, but continuous doesn't imply differentiable (corners, cusps, vertical tangents)
Recognize a limit that IS a derivative: lim_{h→0} [(2 + h)³ − 8]/h = derivative of x³ at x = 2 = 12

concepts.intro: A handful of rules handle most derivatives without using the limit definition.
b: Power rule: d/dx xⁿ = n·xⁿ⁻¹; constants differentiate to 0
Sum and constant-multiple rules let you differentiate term by term
d/dx sin x = cos x, d/dx cos x = −sin x, d/dx eˣ = eˣ, d/dx ln x = 1/x
Product rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg'
Quotient rule: (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g²

concepts.intro: The derivative turns into an equation for the line that best fits the curve at a point.
b: Tangent line at x = a: y − f(a) = f'(a)(x − a)
A horizontal tangent occurs where f'(x) = 0
The normal line is perpendicular to the tangent: slope −1/f'(a)
Local linearization: f(x) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)(x − a) for x near a
More trig derivatives: d/dx tan x = sec² x, d/dx sec x = sec x tan x

concepts.intro: Differentiate compositions from the outside in.
b: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) · g'(x)
d/dx [g(x)]ⁿ = n[g(x)]ⁿ⁻¹ g'(x)
d/dx e^{g(x)} = e^{g(x)} g'(x); d/dx ln g(x) = g'(x)/g(x)
d/dx sin(g(x)) = cos(g(x)) g'(x)
Nested compositions: apply the chain rule once per layer

keyFacts: Power rule: d/dx xⁿ = n xⁿ⁻¹.
Tangent line: y − f(a) = f'(a)(x − a).
traps: (fg)' is not f'g'. Use the product rule.
Quotient rule order matters: the numerator is f'g − fg', not fg' − f'g.
A function can be continuous at a point where it isn't differentiable, like |x| at 0.
Don't forget the inner derivative: d/dx sin(3x) = 3cos(3x), not cos(3x).

units.name: Integration & Differential Equations

concepts.intro: A definite integral adds up a rate over an interval to give total change.
b: ∫_a^b f(x) dx is the signed area between f and the x-axis; area below the axis counts as negative
Left, right and midpoint Riemann sums approximate it with rectangles; the trapezoidal rule uses trapezoids
For an increasing f, a left sum underestimates and a right sum overestimates
The integral of a rate gives net change: ∫_a^b r(t) dt = amount gained from a to b
Properties: ∫_a^a f = 0, ∫_b^a f = −∫_a^b f, and integrals over adjacent intervals add

concepts.intro: Differentiation and integration undo each other.
b: FTC part 2: ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F' = f
FTC part 1: d/dx ∫_a^x f(t) dt = f(x)
With a variable upper limit: d/dx ∫_a^{g(x)} f(t) dt = f(g(x)) g'(x)
Accumulation function: g(x) = g(a) + ∫_a^x g'(t) dt
The FTC turns area and total-change questions into antiderivative problems

concepts.intro: Finding antiderivatives reverses the derivative rules.
b: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C
∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C; ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C
u-substitution reverses the chain rule: let u be the inner function and replace du = u'(x) dx
For definite integrals, change the limits to u-values or substitute back before evaluating
Always include + C for indefinite integrals

concepts.intro: A differential equation relates a function to its derivatives; a slope field sketches its solutions.
b: dy/dx = f(x, y) gives the slope of a solution curve at every point
A slope field draws short segments with those slopes at grid points
Solution curves follow the segments like currents in a stream
Verify a solution by substituting it (and its derivative) into the equation
An initial condition like y(0) = 2 picks out one particular solution

keyFacts: The integral of a rate is net change.
traps: The definite integral is net (signed) area. Total area needs absolute values.
Don't forget + C on indefinite integrals.
With u-substitution in a definite integral, change the limits too.
Add the constant of integration before solving for y, not after exponentiating incorrectly.

units.name: Applications of Integration

concepts.intro: Integrals turn rates into totals and averages.
b: Average value of f on [a, b]: (1/(b − a)) ∫_a^b f(x) dx
Displacement on [a, b] = ∫_a^b v(t) dt
Total distance traveled = ∫_a^b |v(t)| dt
Position: s(b) = s(a) + ∫_a^b v(t) dt
Units: integrating a rate multiplies its units by the input's units (m/s × s = m)

concepts.intro: Subtract the lower curve from the upper curve and integrate.
b: Area = ∫_a^b [top(x) − bottom(x)] dx
Find intersection points to get the limits of integration
If the curves cross, split the integral where top and bottom switch
Integrating with respect to y: ∫ [right(y) − left(y)] dy
Area is always positive, so check which function is on top

concepts.intro: Slice a solid into thin pieces whose volumes you can add up.
b: Disc method: V = π ∫_a^b [R(x)]² dx
Washer method: V = π ∫_a^b ([R(x)]² − [r(x)]²) dx
Radii are distances from the axis of rotation, so adjust when rotating about lines like y = −1
Known cross sections: V = ∫_a^b A(x) dx, with A(x) the area of the cross section (square, semicircle, …)
Square cross sections with side s have A = s²; semicircles with diameter s have A = (π/8)s²

keyFacts: Total distance = ∫ |v(t)| dt; displacement = ∫ v(t) dt.
traps: Displacement and total distance differ when velocity changes sign.
In the washer method it's R² − r², not (R − r)².
The average value of f is not the average of f(a) and f(b).

units.name: Parametric, Polar & Vector Functions

concepts.intro: Parametric curves give x and y separately as functions of a parameter t.
b: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0
d²y/dx² = [d/dt (dy/dx)] / (dx/dt)
Horizontal tangent where dy/dt = 0 (dx/dt ≠ 0); vertical tangent where dx/dt = 0 (dy/dt ≠ 0)
Arc length: L = ∫_a^b √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt
Eliminate the parameter to identify the curve, e.g. x = cos t, y = sin t is the unit circle

concepts.intro: Position, velocity and acceleration can be written as vectors in the plane.
b: Position r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩; velocity v(t) = ⟨x'(t), y'(t)⟩; acceleration a(t) = ⟨x''(t), y''(t)⟩
Speed = |v(t)| = √(x'(t)² + y'(t)²)
Displacement = ∫ v(t) dt componentwise; distance traveled = ∫ speed dt
Position at time b: r(b) = r(a) + ∫_a^b v(t) dt
A particle moves left when x'(t) < 0 and up when y'(t) > 0

concepts.intro: Polar coordinates describe points by distance r and angle θ.
b: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, r² = x² + y²
Area enclosed: A = (1/2) ∫_α^β r² dθ
Area between curves: (1/2) ∫ (r_outer² − r_inner²) dθ
Slope: dy/dx = (dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ) using x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ
Rose curves r = cos(nθ) have n petals if n is odd and 2n if n is even

traps: Polar area uses (1/2)r², not r.
The second derivative for parametric curves divides by dx/dt again.
Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector.

units.name: Infinite Sequences & Series

concepts.intro: A series adds up the terms of a sequence; it converges if its partial sums approach a finite limit.
b: A sequence aₙ converges if lim_{n→∞} aₙ exists
A series Σaₙ converges if the partial sums Sₙ = a₁ + … + aₙ approach a limit
nth-term test: if lim aₙ ≠ 0, the series diverges (if it is 0, the test says nothing)
Geometric series Σ arⁿ converges to a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1 and diverges when |r| ≥ 1
Telescoping series collapse when consecutive terms cancel

concepts.intro: Different series shapes call for different tests.
b: p-series Σ1/nᵖ converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1 (the harmonic series Σ1/n diverges)
Integral test: for positive, decreasing f, Σf(n) and ∫_1^∞ f(x) dx both converge or both diverge
Comparison and limit comparison tests compare to a known series
Ratio test: L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|; L < 1 converges absolutely, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 inconclusive
Alternating series test: if |aₙ| decreases to 0, Σ(−1)ⁿaₙ converges

concepts.intro: Some series converge only because their signs alternate.
b: Absolutely convergent: Σ|aₙ| converges (then Σaₙ converges too)
Conditionally convergent: Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges, e.g. the alternating harmonic series
Alternating series error bound: |S − Sₙ| ≤ |aₙ₊₁|
Choose tests by form: factorials or powers → ratio test; rational functions → p-series comparison
Always name the test and check its conditions when justifying

keyFacts: nth-term test can only prove divergence.
traps: aₙ → 0 does not mean Σaₙ converges (harmonic series).
The ratio test is inconclusive when L = 1.
Conditional convergence needs both: Σaₙ converges and Σ|aₙ| diverges.

units.name: Taylor & Maclaurin Series

concepts.intro: Polynomials built from derivatives at one point approximate a function near that point.
b: Taylor polynomial about x = a: Pₙ(x) = Σ_{k=0}^n f^{(k)}(a)(x − a)ᵏ / k!
Maclaurin means a = 0
The coefficient of (x − a)ᵏ is f^{(k)}(a)/k!, so derivatives can be read off coefficients
Higher degree usually gives a better approximation near a
P₁ is the tangent line; P₂ also matches concavity

concepts.intro: A few series are worth memorizing and adapting.
b: eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … (all x)
sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − … (all x)
cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − … (all x)

concepts.intro: Substitute, multiply, differentiate or integrate known series instead of computing derivatives.
b: Substitute: e^{−x²} = 1 − x² + x⁴/2! − …
Multiply by powers of x: x·sin x = x² − x⁴/3! + …
Differentiate or integrate term by term (the radius of convergence stays the same)
1/(1 + x²) = 1 − x² + x⁴ − …, and integrating gives arctan x = x − x³/3 + x⁵/5 − …
Use series to evaluate limits, e.g. lim_{x→0} (sin x − x)/x³ = −1/6

traps: Don't forget the factorial in each Taylor coefficient.
sin x has only odd powers; cos x has only even powers.
A series only equals its function inside the interval of convergence.

units.name: Polynomial Approximations & Series Convergence

concepts.l: Power Series and Intervals of Convergence
concepts.intro: A power series converges on an interval centered at its center.
b: Σcₙ(x − a)ⁿ converges for |x − a| < R, where R is the radius of convergence
Use the ratio test to find R, then test each endpoint separately
Endpoints can converge absolutely, conditionally, or diverge
Differentiating or integrating term by term keeps R (endpoints may change)
At the center x = a, every power series converges

concepts.intro: The Lagrange bound limits how far a Taylor polynomial can be from the function.
b: M is a bound for |f^{(n+1)}| between a and x
For sin x and cos x, M = 1 always works
Choose n large enough that the bound is below the required accuracy
The bound is a guarantee, not the actual error

concepts.l: Alternating Series Error and Choosing Approximations
concepts.intro: For alternating series with decreasing terms, the next term bounds the error.
b: |S − Sₙ| ≤ |aₙ₊₁| when the terms alternate, decrease in size and approach 0
The sign of the first omitted term tells whether the partial sum over- or underestimates
Example: sin(0.1) ≈ 0.1 − 0.1³/6 with error < 0.1⁵/120
Use the alternating bound when the series alternates; otherwise use Lagrange
Approximating integrals: integrate the Taylor polynomial, then bound the error

keyFacts: Radius from the ratio test; always check endpoints separately.
Every power series converges at its center.
traps: The ratio test never decides the endpoints. Test them separately.
In Lagrange, M bounds the (n + 1)th derivative, not the nth.
The alternating bound needs decreasing terms.

PART_B2.q: A particle moves with x(t) = t² − 2t and y(t) = t³/3 for t ≥ 0. (a) Find the velocity vector at t = 3. (b) Find the speed at t = 3. (c) At what time is the tangent line vertical? (d) Write an integral for the distance traveled from t = 0 to t = 3.
PART_B2.sa: (a) v = ⟨2t − 2, t²⟩ = ⟨4, 9⟩. (b) √(16 + 81) = √97. (c) x'(t) = 0 at t = 1, and y'(1) = 1 ≠ 0, so the tangent is vertical at t = 1. (d) ∫_0^3 √((2t − 2)² + t⁴) dt.

PART_B2.q: Consider f(x) = Σ_{n=1}^∞ (x − 2)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ). (a) Find the interval of convergence. (b) Find the first three nonzero terms of f'(x). (c) Is f(1) convergent absolutely or conditionally?
PART_B2.sa: (a) Ratio test: |x − 2|/3 < 1 → −1 < x < 5. At x = 5: Σ1/n diverges. At x = −1: Σ(−1)ⁿ/n converges. Interval: [−1, 5). (b) f'(x) = Σ (x − 2)ⁿ⁻¹/3ⁿ = 1/3 + (x − 2)/9 + (x − 2)²/27 + …. (c) At x = 1, (x − 2)ⁿ = (−1)ⁿ, so f(1) = Σ(−1)ⁿ/(n·3ⁿ). The absolute values Σ1/(n·3ⁿ) converge by comparison with Σ(1/3)ⁿ, so f(1) converges absolutely.

PART_C.q: Consider dy/dx = x/y with y(0) = 3 (y > 0). (a) Find d²y/dx² in terms of x and y. (b) Find the particular solution. (c) Use the tangent line at x = 0 to approximate y(0.2).
PART_C.sa: (a) d²y/dx² = (y − x·y')/y² = (y − x²/y)/y² = (y² − x²)/y³. (b) y dy = x dx → y²/2 = x²/2 + C; y(0) = 3 gives C = 9/2, so y = √(x² + 9). (c) At (0, 3), slope = 0/3 = 0, so y(0.2) ≈ 3.

PART_C.q: Let R be the region bounded by y = √x, y = 0 and x = 4. (a) Find the area of R. (b) Find the volume when R is rotated about the x-axis. (c) Write, but don't evaluate, an integral for the volume when R is rotated about the line y = 2.
PART_C.sa: (a) ∫_0^4 √x dx = (2/3)(8) = 16/3. (b) π∫_0^4 x dx = 8π. (c) Washer about y = 2: outer radius 2 − 0 = 2, inner radius 2 − √x, so V = π∫_0^4 [2² − (2 − √x)²] dx.
